current_definition: Ruling or behaving as if one holds complete power and no one else's opinion matters—unwilling to share control or be questioned by anyone.
To force someone to do something by threatening them with punishment, violence, or serious harm if they refuse—they comply not by choice but out of fear.
A ruler who holds absolute, unchecked power and uses it harshly—without elections, legal limits, or accountability to anyone.
The dominance of one country, group, or institution over others—exercised not always by direct force, but through political pressure, economic power, or cultural influence.
Relating to an empire or its ruler—describing laws, authority, or ambitions that belong to or come from an empire.
Relating to war, soldiers, or the military—used for anything connected with armed force, combat, or military authority.
To calm someone who is angry, upset, or difficult—to bring them to a quieter, more manageable state.
To succeed or win, especially against difficulty or strong opposition.
To officially ban something—to declare it forbidden by law or authority so that no one is permitted to do or use it.
To bring a people, nation, or group under complete control by force—to defeat them so thoroughly that they have no choice but to obey.
To take power, a position, or a right that belongs to someone else—usually by force or deception, and without any legal right to do so.
Belonging to the highest social class—the nobility—by birth or family title.

(adjective) Relating to the middle class, especially in a way that suggests conventional thinking, comfort-seeking, and material values. (noun) A member of the middle class, particularly one seen as overly focused on property and social respectability.
To speak or behave as though you are better than the person you are dealing with—treating them as less intelligent or less important.
A person, animal, or plant that lives in or regularly occupies a particular place—used to describe any established inhabitant of a specific environment.
Polite and refined in a way that suggests good social standing; sometimes used with a hint of mockery—suggesting someone is trying too hard to appear respectable.
A system in which people, groups, or things are ranked one above another according to power, status, or importance—with the most powerful at the top and the least powerful at the bottom.
Originating naturally in a particular place and having lived or existed there since before others arrived—native to a region, not brought in from outside.
(adjective) Belonging to or typical of the upper class—refined, cultured, and accustomed to privilege. (noun) A member of the highest social class; historically, a member of the Roman nobility.
To speak to or treat someone as though they are less intelligent or capable than they are—often without realizing you are doing it.

(adjective) Relating to ordinary people rather than the upper class; sometimes used to suggest a lack of culture or refinement. (noun) A common person—in ancient Rome, any citizen who was not a patrician; more broadly, someone from the lower social orders.
The working class—those who earn wages by their labour, typically in manual or industrial work, and who own no significant property or capital.
A distinct layer or level within a larger structure—in social terms, a recognisable class or group defined by income, education, or status.
To give up a throne or the highest position of power—to step down formally from a role of supreme authority.
A position of growing or established dominance over others—the state of having power or influence that is clearly rising or firmly held.
To officially declare something sacred or holy through a religious ceremony—setting it apart for divine use.
A sudden seizure of power from a government—usually carried out by a small group such as the military, and often without warning or a popular vote.
To reach the highest or final point after a process of building or development—to end in a particular outcome after a long lead-up.
To formally install someone in a position of authority through an official ceremony.
Something handed down from a person, era, or event—whether money, property, ideas, or lasting consequences—that continues to shape the present long after its source is gone.
To officially require or order that something be done.

(verb) To organise people, facts, or resources carefully and deliberately—especially in preparation for an effort or argument. (noun) A high-ranking military officer or a law-enforcement official with senior authority.
Better than all others in a particular field or area—the most respected, distinguished, or important of its kind.
To act before someone else can, in order to prevent what they were planning to do—or to replace something before it happens by doing something first.
To make a new law, rule, or official decision publicly known and formally put into effect—to announce it as binding authority.
A state in which there is no working government or law—where normal social order has broken down and no authority is in control. More broadly, any situation of complete disorder and confusion.
A place, person, or institution that strongly defends a particular belief, way of life, or set of values—a last strong point of resistance against change or attack.
A deep, wide gap between two things—used literally for a physical gap in the earth, and figuratively for a large and serious division between people, groups, or ideas.
A small, organised group within a larger organisation—one that has its own goals and often pushes against the main group's leadership or direction.
To stir up or encourage the development of something dangerous or violent—especially trouble, rebellion, or unrest—by feeding people's anger or dissatisfaction.

(noun) A person who takes up arms or organises resistance against their own government or an occupying force—not yet recognised as a formal army. (adjective) Describing such a person or the movement they belong to.
A person who suffers greatly or dies for a belief, cause, or religion—and whose suffering makes them a symbol that inspires others to continue the same fight.
To divide people or opinion into two sharply opposed and hostile camps, with very little middle ground left between them.
The main character in a story, film, or play—the central figure whose actions drive the plot.
Stubbornly refusing to obey, cooperate, or change—resisting authority or instruction even when direct pressure is applied.
Speech, writing, or action intended to encourage people to rebel against or disobey the authority of the state—not yet open revolt, but deliberate effort to undermine the government's power.

(adjective) Intended to secretly weaken or destroy an established system, government, or set of values—working against authority from the inside rather than through open confrontation. (noun) A person who works in this way.

An economic system in which businesses, factories, and property are owned by private individuals rather than the state—and in which profit, competition, and market prices determine what is produced and how wealth is distributed.
Rigidly committed to a set of ideas or principles, and unwilling to adjust them to fit reality—applying a doctrine even when the facts clearly argue against it.
Stating beliefs as though they are absolute facts that cannot be questioned or doubted—refusing to consider any other view or any evidence to the contrary.
(adjective) Believing in or promoting the principle that all people are equal and deserve equal rights, opportunities, and treatment. (noun) A person who holds this belief.
To publicly adopt, support, and promote a belief, cause, or set of ideas—to commit yourself to it openly and speak up for it.
A complete set of ideas and beliefs—about how society should be organised, who should hold power, and what is just—that forms the basis of a political movement or system.
A public declaration in which a person, party, or movement sets out its goals, beliefs, and plans—especially before an election or at the start of a campaign.
Conforming to the accepted, established, or traditional beliefs of a religion, field, or group—not questioning or departing from the standard view.

(adjective) Strongly supporting one side or party in a dispute, with little interest in fairness to the other side. (noun) A committed supporter of a cause or party; also, a member of an armed resistance group fighting against an occupying force.

(noun) A forceful, aggressive piece of writing or speech that attacks an opposing view, person, or institution—not trying to be fair, but trying to win the argument and discredit the other side. (adjective) Describing such writing or speech.
A person who actively supports and argues in favour of a particular idea, plan, or cause—someone who promotes it and tries to convince others.
A core belief or principle that forms part of a larger set of ideas—one of the fundamental points that a religion, movement, or system is built on.
A list of items to be discussed or dealt with at a meeting or during a period of activity.
Clever trickery or deliberate deception used to gain an advantage—skill applied not to make something but to fool someone.
A small, tight group of people who socialise mostly with each other and deliberately exclude others—giving outsiders the impression they are not welcome.
Secret cooperation between two or more parties to achieve something dishonest or illegal—especially when they are supposed to be acting independently or against each other.
Involvement in or shared responsibility for a wrongdoing—knowing that something bad is happening and helping it along, even if you are not the one doing it directly.
Done in secret and deliberately hidden from public view—especially used for official or organised activities that are kept concealed.
Done quickly and quietly to avoid being noticed—behaving as though you have something to hide, with nervous, secretive movements or glances.
Spreading or developing slowly and harmfully in a way that is hard to notice until serious damage has already been done—dangerous precisely because it does not look dangerous at first.
A secret and clever scheme to achieve a goal, usually by manipulating people or events behind the scenes—always implies dishonest or self-serving intent. Often used in the plural.
Owned by a specific company or person and protected by law—not available for others to use, copy, or sell without permission.
Done in a way that is kept carefully hidden, especially because it would not be approved of if seen—acting in secret to avoid detection.
Full of anger, bitterness, and hostility—used to describe an argument, relationship, or split in which deep resentment is openly expressed.
So obvious and openly done that it cannot be missed or denied—said of something bad that the person doing it does not even try to hide.
To criticise someone very severely and harshly—usually in public and using strong language that makes clear how seriously they have failed or wronged others.
Deserving blame for something wrong or harmful—responsible for a fault or failure, whether through direct action or through negligence.
To officially clear someone of blame or a criminal charge—to formally state that they are not responsible for what they were accused of.
Shockingly obvious and done without any attempt at concealment—used for wrongs so open and bold that they show complete disregard for rules or decency.
Deep public shame and disgrace—the humiliation of having your reputation destroyed in front of others, especially after a serious failure or moral wrongdoing.
Well known for something bad, criminal, or morally shocking—famous in a negative sense, where the reputation is built entirely on wrongdoing or scandal.
Widely known and talked about because of something bad—having a reputation that is established and recognised far beyond the original offence or scandal.
Deserving very strong moral criticism—so wrong that it cannot be excused or defended, and any decent person should condemn it.
To mark or treat a person or group as shameful, inferior, or unacceptable—in a way that becomes a lasting social label that follows them in public life.

Behaviour that is deeply immoral, wicked, or corrupt—used especially in legal and formal contexts to describe conduct so dishonest or depraved that it disqualifies a person from holding a position of trust.
A person who supports and follows a particular leader, belief, movement, or set of ideas—committed enough to identify themselves with it publicly.
To persuade someone to do something by using flattery, gentle pressure, or repeated coaxing—not by force, but by wearing down resistance with persistent charm.
Respectful submission to the wishes, judgment, or authority of another—choosing to follow their lead rather than assert your own view, out of respect for their position or expertise.
Quiet, obedient, and easy to manage or control—willing to follow instructions without resistance or complaint.
In name only—holding a title or position without the real power, authority, or substance that the title suggests.
Excessively eager to please or obey someone in authority—flattering and submissive to the point where it becomes obvious and unpleasant to watch.
Annoyingly eager to give orders, enforce rules, or interfere in other people's affairs—especially when you have no real authority to do so.
To express disapproval of someone's behaviour, usually in a mild or calm way—not a harsh punishment, but a clear signal that what they did was wrong.
Excessively eager to serve or obey others—behaving as though your only purpose is to please those above you, with no independent will or self-respect.
A person who flatters and agrees with someone powerful in order to gain favour—saying what that person wants to hear rather than what is true or useful.
To take something for one's own use, typically without the owner's permission; to officially allocate money or resources for a specific purpose.
Having the freedom to act independently; self-governing; not controlled by others.
A system of government or management with complex rules and processes; excessive official paperwork and regulation.
To reduce or limit something; to impose a restriction that cuts something short.
A wealthy and influential person, especially in business or industry; a powerful figure in a particular field.
The practice of favoring relatives or close friends when giving jobs or other advantages, especially in a position of power.
Of or relating to a father; showing fatherly protection, concern, or guidance; characteristic of a caring but controlling authority.
The male head of a family or tribe; a man who is the founder or dominant figure of a community or organization.
Insisting on immediate attention or obedience in a brusquely imperious way; not allowing contradiction or refusal.
A benefit or privilege granted to an employee in addition to their salary; something regarded as a special right attached to a position.
A right or privilege exclusive to a particular individual or class; a special power or authority.
A person or thing that acts as a substitute for another; a deputy or replacement serving in place of the original.
Having a great deal of money and material wealth; prosperous and comfortable in financial terms.
A desirable or useful feature or facility that adds comfort or convenience to a place; a pleasant or agreeable aspect.
Of or relating to cooking, food preparation, or the kitchen; pertaining to the art or practice of cookery.
Luxuriously self-indulgent; characterized by moral or cultural decline through excessive pleasure-seeking.
To display something ostentatiously, especially wealth or possessions, in order to attract attention or provoke envy.
Extravagantly large, ambitious, or impressive; seemingly impressive but in a way that is excessive or absurd.
Larger or more generous than is usual or necessary; characterised by lavish generosity.
Ostentatiously rich and luxurious; demonstrating wealth through lavish display of resources.
Characterised by a vulgar or pretentious display of wealth and resources, primarily designed to impress or attract notice.
Having assets in excess of liabilities; financially stable and able to meet all monetary obligations.
Experienced or present to the most extreme degree; utterly hopeless or degrading; completely without pride or dignity.
Extreme greed for wealth or material gain; an insatiable desire to accumulate riches.
To yearn intensely to possess or have something belonging to another person; to desire enviously.
A scarcity or insufficient quantity of something; a serious lack of a needed resource or supply.
An excessively abundant supply of something, typically more than the market or demand can absorb.
Impossible to satisfy regardless of how much is given; having an unlimited or unquenchable desire.
Primarily concerned with making money at the expense of ethics; motivated by financial gain above all other considerations.
The presence of something only in small or insufficient quantities; a serious scarcity of what is needed.
Aggressively greedy or grasping; plundering and seizing by force; voraciously acquisitive.
To waste money, time, or resources in a reckless or foolish manner; to allow something valuable to be lost through neglect.
Extremely bad or appalling; so deep or severe as to seem immeasurably hopeless or terrible.
Without the basic necessities of life; in a state of extreme poverty with no financial resources whatsoever.
Poor and needy; lacking the basic necessities of life; in a condition of extreme financial want.
A person who lives by begging; one who depends entirely on charity or alms for survival.
Contemptibly small or inadequate in amount; trivial and of little value or significance.
Involving immoral or dishonest activities; dirty, filthy, or wretched in condition; ignoble in nature.
A state of being extremely dirty and unpleasant, especially as a result of poverty or neglect; filth and wretchedness.
A state of inactivity or lack of development; failure to flow, move, or progress.
Based on personal whim or random choice rather than any clear rule, reason, or fairness.
Careful to think through all possible consequences before acting or speaking; cautious and watchful.
A person with deep knowledge and refined taste in a particular subject, especially art, food, or music.
A standard or rule used to judge, evaluate, or make a decision about something.
To see, notice, or understand something that is not immediately obvious, often through careful observation or thought.
To recognize and understand the difference between two or more things; to tell them apart with care.
To notice or point out what makes one thing different from another.
Fair and impartial to everyone involved, giving each person what they reasonably deserve.
Demanding very high standards and close attention to every detail; not willing to accept anything less than the best.
So clear and well-reasoned that it is hard to argue against; powerfully convincing.
Very attentive to cleanliness, accuracy, or quality, sometimes to a degree that others find excessive.
Showing good sense and careful thought when making decisions; wise and well-considered.
Expressed in a way that is very easy to understand; clear and organized in thought or language.
Done with extremely careful attention to every small detail, requiring great effort and patience.
Directly related to or useful for the subject being discussed or considered.
To meet the necessary requirements or standards needed for something.
Extremely thorough and demanding, leaving no room for error or shortcuts.
Having or showing a deep ability to understand things and make good decisions; wise in a practical way.
Extremely careful to be honest and to do what is morally right; also used to mean very precise and thorough.
Wild, excessive behavior involving alcohol, pleasure, and self-indulgence carried to a harmful or shameful degree.
To slowly fall to a lower, worse, or more harmful condition than before.
A state of deep moral corruption; wicked or evil behavior that goes far beyond normal wrongdoing.
To gradually waste or spend money, energy, or resources until nothing is left.
Not allowed by law or by the rules of society; forbidden and usually done in secret.
Wrongdoing or illegal action carried out by someone in a position of official power or public trust.
Wicked and criminal in a way that is openly shocking; morally outrageous.
A deliberate act of betrayal by someone who was trusted; breaking faith with those who relied on you.
Recklessly wasteful with money or resources; also used to describe someone with no moral restraint.
To officially declare that someone is free from blame, guilt, or punishment; to release a person from an obligation or responsibility.
To make a problem, pain, or bad feeling less severe, without removing it completely.
Mercy or leniency shown toward someone who could be punished severely; a decision to reduce or forgive a penalty.
To accept or allow behaviour that most people consider wrong, either by saying nothing or by approving of it openly.
Feeling or showing deep, sincere sorrow for having done something wrong; genuinely sorry and ashamed.
Too willing to allow or forgive bad behaviour; giving people whatever they want without setting firm limits.
A small, unimportant fault or sin; a minor act of wrongdoing that people do not usually take very seriously.
Feeling sorry for doing wrong and willing to accept punishment or do whatever is needed to make things right.
Something done or paid to make up for harm or damage caused; compensation given to people who have been wronged.
A short break from something difficult, painful, or unpleasant; a brief period of relief before something hard continues.
To go beyond an accepted limit or rule; to do something that is morally or legally wrong.
So wrong or unfair that no reasonable person could accept it; going far beyond what is morally or legally allowable.
To warn or firmly advise someone that their behaviour is wrong, usually in a calm but serious way; to tell someone off without harsh punishment.
An official, formal statement or act declaring that someone has behaved wrongly; to issue such a statement against someone.
To criticise or punish someone harshly, especially after they have done something wrong; to scold in a forceful, sometimes harsh way.
To openly disobey or show no respect for a rule, law, or accepted standard, often in a bold or deliberate way.
An official order from a court or authority that commands someone to do something or, more often, to stop doing something.
A sharp, direct expression of disapproval given by someone in authority; to speak to someone in a way that makes clear their behaviour was wrong.
A feeling or expression of disappointment and disapproval directed at someone; to express that feeling to someone directly.
A harsh critical comment directed at a person's behaviour or work.
Gentle, kind, and unlikely to cause harm; having a pleasant and harmless effect on others.
Polite and respectful in behaviour, especially toward people one disagrees with; meeting the basic standard of good manners.
Behaving in a way that is proper, calm, and appropriate for the situation; showing good taste and self-control in conduct.
So perfect that no fault can be found; meeting the highest possible standard in every detail.
Completely harmless; unlikely to upset, offend, or cause any damage to anyone.
Very generous and forgiving, especially toward someone who has done wrong or who is in a weaker position; showing a noble, big-hearted spirit.
In perfect, original condition, with nothing damaged, spoiled, or corrupted; completely clean and unspoiled.
Producing a good or useful effect, especially by serving as a warning or lesson; beneficial even if it feels uncomfortable.
Of such outstanding quality, beauty, or greatness that it seems almost beyond what is normally possible; causing deep admiration or wonder.
Completely unwilling to change one's mind or position, no matter what arguments or pressure are applied.
So set in bad habits or a fixed way of behaving that no punishment, correction, or persuasion can bring about change.
Refusing to compromise or reach any agreement; holding a position so firmly that no middle ground is possible.
Having a habit, attitude, or way of life so deeply fixed over a long time that it is almost impossible to change.
Never stopping or letting up; continuing with full force despite difficulties, setbacks, or the passage of time.
Having a firm, clear purpose and the steady determination to carry it through, especially when facing opposition or hardship.
Strong and sturdy in body or in construction; able to withstand rough conditions without breaking down.
Loyal and committed to a person, cause, or belief in a way that does not waver even under serious pressure.
Holding on to a goal, belief, or position with great determination and refusing to let go even when the situation becomes very difficult.
The willingness to do or say something that most people would consider shockingly bold or rude; reckless daring.
A strong feeling that someone or something is far beneath you and not worth your time or respect.
Thinking only of oneself and one's own needs, interests, and views, with little or no awareness of how others feel.
Extreme admiration of oneself — one's looks, abilities, or importance — to a degree that leaves little room for genuine care about others.
To create a strong, favorable impression on someone right from the first moment; to charm or win over immediately.
Constantly complaining or finding fault in a whiny, irritable way, often about small or unimportant things.
Using humor or remarks that are mocking and a little cruel, showing that you think little of the person or situation you are commenting on.
Behaving as though you believe you are far superior to the people around you and that they barely deserve your attention.
The willingness to do something that is dangerously bold or disrespectful, especially when it is likely to cause serious trouble or offence.
Eager, cheerful readiness and quickness to act or respond, with no sign of reluctance or hesitation.
Feeling or showing something — a belief, a desire, an emotion — with great intensity and passion; deeply committed or enthusiastic.
Changing one's mind, mood, or direction suddenly and without clear reason, making it very hard for others to predict what comes next.
Quick to become angry; having a temperament that moves easily into irritation or rage, often over minor things.
Intense, deeply felt enthusiasm or passion for a cause, belief, or activity — strong enough that it shows clearly in how a person speaks or acts.
Moving, happening, or working at a wild, almost out-of-control speed, as if driven by too much nervous energy to slow down.
Acting suddenly on a feeling or idea without stopping to think about the consequences; driven by strong impulse rather than careful thought.
Having a very short temper; easily and quickly angered, especially by small frustrations or delays.
Changing mood, opinion, or behavior very quickly and unpredictably, so that those around you never know quite what to expect next.
Showing childish, sulky bad temper when something does not go the way you want, often over a small or trivial matter.
Cool and distant in manner; not friendly or interested in mixing with others.
A strong, lasting feeling of dislike or opposition toward someone or something.
Lacking confidence in oneself; hesitant to speak up or put oneself forward.
A calm, steady state of mind that does not change even in difficult or stressful situations.
Having no particular interest in or concern about something; neither for nor against.
Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or feelings, even when pressured or given good reasons.
Preferring to live or spend time alone and away from other people; deliberately avoiding company.
Unwilling to talk openly about one's thoughts, feelings, or personal matters.
Enduring pain, hardship, or difficulty without complaining or showing emotion.
Understood or agreed upon without being said out loud; implied rather than stated directly.
A person who speaks very little by nature; habitually quiet and not inclined to conversation.
Easy to talk to and pleasant in manner; friendly and approachable with everyone.
Having a kind, good-natured character that makes people like you and feel comfortable around you.
Working with great care, effort, and persistence over a long period of time; extremely thorough and diligent.
Kind, warm, and gently helpful toward younger or less experienced people, in the way a friendly uncle might be.
A natural ability to attract, inspire, or charm people through one's personality, energy, or presence.
Pleasant and suited to one's tastes or personality; agreeable in company or in atmosphere.
Supremely skilled; showing the highest level of ability achieved through long training and experience.
Lively, friendly, and enjoying the company of others, especially in a social setting with food or drink.
To try to match or be as good as someone admired, by copying their methods or working just as hard.
Showing the kind of warm friendship, loyalty, and support that exists between brothers.
Naturally enjoying being with other people; lively and sociable in groups.
Polite, smooth, and confident in social situations in a way that seems effortless and sophisticated.
A natural feeling of being drawn to or connected with someone or something; a sense of belonging together.
To become fully absorbed into a new culture or group, adopting its customs, language, and way of life.
To come together in a group in one place, usually for a shared purpose or out of shared interest.
Comfortable with and made up of people and ideas from many different countries and cultures; at home in the wider world.
To leave one's home country permanently in order to settle and live in another country.
A person who lives outside their home country, usually for work or personal choice, often for an extended time.
A person who gains energy from being around other people and feels most alive in social situations.
To come into a new country to live there permanently, having left one's home country behind.
The ability to make quick, accurate judgments and smart decisions, especially in a particular field.
Having a sharp, perceptive mind; quick to notice and understand things clearly.
Clever and skilful in using the mind or hands; handling difficult situations with ease and intelligence.
A natural ability or talent for learning or doing something well, often evident from an early age.
Having the ability to understand a situation quickly and use it to one's advantage; mentally sharp in a practical way.
Relating to intellectual thought rather than emotion or physical action; requiring or showing careful mental effort.
Skilled and nimble with the hands or, more broadly, with the mind; also spelled dextrous (both forms are correct and interchangeable).
Having or showing deep, wide-ranging knowledge gained through extensive reading and study.
Intelligently clear and direct; cutting straight to the heart of a matter without unnecessary words.
Highly competent and skilled at something as a result of practice and experience.
Immature and inexperienced, lacking the judgment that comes with age and real-world exposure.
Done quickly and without proper attention to detail; hasty and therefore incomplete or unreliable.
A person who takes up an art, science, or subject as a casual interest rather than as a serious pursuit, resulting in only shallow knowledge.
Appearing neat and clever on the surface but lacking real depth, thought, or effort; too easy to be trustworthy.
Awkward and lacking social grace; behaving in a way that is tactless or embarrassingly unsophisticated.
Using overly elaborate, pompous language designed to impress rather than to communicate clearly.
Added without good reason; uncalled for and unnecessary, often to an offensive or excessive degree.
Lacking the skill or competence to do something; notably clumsy or incompetent.
Overly concerned with minor rules, technical details, or formal correctness in a way that misses the broader point.
Carried out with minimal effort and no genuine care, as a mere formality or out of habit rather than real intent.
A person who is indifferent or openly hostile to culture, art, and intellectual life, preferring only what is practical or commercial.
Concerned only with what is obvious or on the surface; lacking depth of understanding, feeling, or analysis.
Severe mental or emotional suffering, often caused by loss, fear, or a painful situation with no easy resolution.
Feeling worried and uneasy about something that may happen in the future; anticipating trouble or danger.
In a state of deep grief following the death of a loved one; having recently suffered such a loss.
To trouble or afflict someone persistently and from all sides, leaving little room for escape or relief.
To make someone feel intimidated or discouraged, especially when facing a difficult or overwhelming challenge.
Deeply unhappy and without hope; feeling that the situation will not improve and that efforts are useless.
To express deep sorrow, regret, or grief, especially over something that has been lost or cannot be changed.
Mournful and gloomy in an exaggerated or theatrical way; looking or sounding sorrowful to a marked degree.
Sullen, gloomy, and not willing to talk or smile; withdrawn into a silent, unhappy state.
To make someone feel anxious, unsettled, or mentally disturbed, usually by something unexpected or troubling.
Having a sad, mournful quality, especially in sound; expressing sorrow in a way that is gentle rather than angry.
A feeling of fear or anxiety about something that is about to happen; a nervous uncertainty about the future.
Showing signs that something good or successful is likely to happen; giving a promising start.
Cheerful and carefree, showing a light and happy spirit.
Overflowing with enthusiasm, energy, and high spirits; very lively and cheerful.
To feel or show great joy and triumph, especially after a success or victory.
A state of deep happiness and contentment.
The period in a person's life or an era when they were most successful, popular, or powerful.
A light, humorous attitude toward something; the quality of treating serious matters with fun or playfulness.
Giving a good chance of success; favourable to a particular outcome or event.
Optimistic, especially when facing difficulty; cheerfully confident that things will turn out well.
The experience of finding something good or valuable by chance, without having looked for it.
To feel a very strong hatred or disgust toward something, finding it deeply offensive or wrong.
Having a sharp, bitter, and unpleasant smell or taste that irritates the senses.
A strong feeling of hostility or active dislike directed at another person or group.
To cause persistent trouble, worry, or difficulty for someone; to put someone under constant pressure or attack.
Eager or quick to argue, fight, or show aggression; openly hostile in manner or attitude.
Showing a rude lack of respect, especially toward someone in authority; boldly disrespectful.
Deep, lasting bitterness or ill will, especially from a past injury or injustice that has not been forgiven.
An act of harm or punishment carried out in retaliation for something done by another person or group.
Angry or violent conflict between people or groups; a state of ongoing disagreement and struggle.
A complete lack of interest, feeling, or motivation; the state of not caring about things that normally matter.
Feeling so satisfied with one's current situation that one stops trying to improve or stays unaware of possible problems.
To drain someone of energy, strength, or vitality, leaving them feeling weak and unable to act.
Habitually lazy and reluctant to make any effort; avoiding activity or work without a pressing reason.
Unable or unwilling to move or act; lacking all energy or motivation.
To lose strength and vitality over time; to exist in a state of weakness, neglect, or inactivity without improvement.
Feeling sluggish, drowsy, and unable to find the energy to act or think clearly; affected by a lack of vitality.
A state of physical or mental sluggishness and lack of energy that makes it hard to think or act normally.
Slow, dull, and showing very little thought or feeling; resembling the placid, unresponsive nature of cattle.
Following the accepted customs, standards, or ideas of a society; not original or daring.
Done without a clear plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another in a half-hearted way.
Temporarily inactive, sleeping, or not developing, but capable of becoming active again.
A general feeling of unease, dissatisfaction, or lack of energy that is difficult to name or explain precisely.
The state of being completely forgotten, especially by the public or by history.
Extreme laziness and unwillingness to make any effort; a persistent reluctance to work or act.
Causing or tending to cause drowsiness or sleep; so dull that it makes a person lose concentration.
Not moving, changing, or developing; remaining in the same condition over a long period.
